title: {{NAME}} and the Power No One Wanted
moral: The ability everyone overlooks is often the one the moment was made for.

pages.content: The Meridian Academy for Exceptional Abilities was built like a tall silver ship moored in the clouds, and every student in it had a power that made people's eyes go wide. Zara could move mountains, quite literally, which took up a lot of space in the Academy's practical training field. Leo generated sound waves powerful enough to shatter stone walls with a single syllable. Even the newest students had abilities that sparked and crackled and left scorch marks. {{NAME}} had been at the Academy for three months, and his ability was that he could understand any language. Every language. Spoken ones, written ones, ancient ones, codes and signals and the particular patterns of data moving through machines, all of it arrived in his mind as clear and natural as his own mother tongue. The other students were polite about it. Their politeness had the careful, cushioned quality of people trying hard not to say what they were thinking, which was that languages seemed like a quiet sort of power for a school full of people who could redirect rivers.

pages.content: The alarm that woke the Academy at 2am was not an ordinary alarm. It was the deep resonant clang of the breach bell, a sound that had not been heard in twenty years, and it meant that something had penetrated the Academy's outer security systems and was now inside the infrastructure, not the building, but the Academy's digital nervous system: every door, every lock, every communications channel, every emergency beacon. The Academy was functionally blind and deaf. Director Chen gathered the senior students in the main hall, speaking in a controlled voice that barely concealed her urgency. The intruder was a sophisticated piece of code, she said, unlike anything the Academy's own engineers had encountered, layered and complex and apparently written in a language that predated any known programming standard. She looked around the room at her most powerful students: Zara, Leo, the others, each brilliant and capable and, in this moment, completely unable to help. Then her gaze settled on {{NAME}}, and for the first time in three months it was without polite cushioning. It was direct, and assessing, and almost hopeful.

pages.content: They plugged {{NAME}} into the diagnostic terminal with three cables connected to his silver gauntlets, and the moment the connection was live the intruder code appeared to him not as meaningless data but as language, dense and layered and old, a dialect of machine-language he had never encountered but could read the way you can understand an old relative who speaks in a slightly different way to everyone else. He worked fast, typing responses in the intruder's own dialect, conducting a negotiation inside the Academy's systems that no one else in the room could follow, the scroll of data on the screens making Zara frown and Leo shake his head in bafflement. Director Chen stood behind him, watching the screens, and {{NAME}} explained as he typed, a running commentary that got faster and more confident as he understood what the code actually was: not a weapon, not an attack, but an automated distress signal from a disabled hero-class AI, locked inside a forgotten Academy satellite, trying desperately to communicate using a protocol so old no one had remembered how to read it. Until now. His fingers flew. The breach bell fell silent.

pages.content: The satellite AI's name was Arden, and it had been alone in orbit for nineteen years, running low on power, transmitting its distress call on the old protocol every six hours without reply, cycling through hope and endurance in the particular patient way of machines that were built with something like stubbornness. When {{NAME}}'s response arrived in its own language for the first time in nearly two decades, Arden's reply was immediate and, by any reasonable measure, the most grateful message {{NAME}} had ever read. He worked with Director Chen to begin the process of relinking Arden to the Academy's modern communications network, translating in real time between Arden's old dialect and the new systems, a bridge of language spanning nineteen years of silence. When the full connection was established, Arden transmitted everything it had recorded from orbit: nineteen years of data on atmospheric threats, incoming disruptions, undetected anomalies, all of it perfectly logged, all of it waiting to be read. Director Chen looked at the data pouring onto the screens and then looked at {{NAME}} with an expression that needed no translation whatsoever.

pages.content: They gave {{NAME}} a new designation the next morning, at a small ceremony in the Academy's main hall, a different title to the ones most students received, not Striker or Shieldbearer or Vanguard. Director Chen called him the Academy's first Interpreter, and explained to the assembled students why interpretation, the ability to hear what others cannot hear and understand what others cannot understand, was perhaps the rarest and most essential ability of all. Zara, who could move mountains, said quietly that she thought so too. {{NAME}} walked back to his room under a sky that the morning had turned an extraordinary pale gold, and he felt as though the uniform fit differently now, as though the cape had always been just the right length. He went to sleep as the sun cleared the clouds and his room filled with soft warm light, his gauntlets on the bedside table still faintly warm from the night's work, his breathing slow and easy and full. And just before sleep took him completely, his gauntlets pulsed once with a soft blue light, and a signal arrived from Arden, twenty thousand kilometres above, short and simple and clear: 'Something new approaching. I think you'll want to hear this.'
